claims.claim_text: Wallach documents that specific mineral deficiencies produced specific deficiency diseases in distinct geographic regions — each disease appeared wherever the local soil lacked that mineral. His examples: iodine deficiency caused goiter (a swollen thyroid) in communities far from the sea; selenium deficiency caused Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle), in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency caused pica (a compulsive craving to eat non-food substances) in South Africa; and copper deficiency caused enzootic ataxia (a copper-deficiency disorder of movement and coordination) in Australia. In his words: "Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia) was common in Australia, etc."

claims.claim_text: Wallach's health framework is built on an unusually large base of comparative pathology. As a pathologist for a multi-institution research program - The Center for the Biology of Natural Systems, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) along with several zoos and universities - he performed autopsies on a scale almost no one else has: more than 20,000 of them, spanning over 17,500 captive wild, laboratory, and domestic animals across more than 454 species, plus 3,000 humans for comparison. That vast cross-species record is what led him to his central claim - that creatures dying of so-called "natural causes" were really dying of nutritional deficiency diseases. In his words: "As a comparative pathologist, I (Wallach) performed more than 20,000 autopsies of over 17,500 captive wild animals, laboratory species and domestic animals, of over 454 species and 3,000 humans for a comparison."

claims.claim_text: Wallach's stance on carbohydrates and sugars: they are not essential nutrients. His reasoning is that the body can make all the carbohydrate and sugar it needs - for energy, upkeep, and structural repair - by breaking down and rebuilding fats and proteins inside the cell, so none has to come from the diet. This runs counter to the popular view of carbohydrates as a required food group. In his words: "Contrary to popular belief, carbohydrates and sugars are not essential nutrients by anybody's standards, as we can make all of the carbohydrates and sugars we need for energy and maintenance and repair of structural components by breaking down and reconfiguring fats and proteins at the cellular level."

claims.claim_text: Wallach counts 12 essential amino acids - the protein building blocks the body cannot make for itself and so must obtain from food: valine, tyrosine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, histidine, phenylalanine, arginine, taurine, and leucine. (Mainstream nutrition usually lists nine; Wallach's list adds tyrosine, arginine, taurine, and histidine.) He warns that if any essential amino acid is missing from the diet for any length of time, a specific - sometimes reversible - deficiency disease results. A footnote adds that selenium researcher Dr. Gerhard Schrauzer considered selenomethionine (the selenium form of methionine) a 13th essential amino acid. In his words: "There are 12 amino acids that are required by the body as protein building blocks, and because the body is unable to manufacture them, they are termed 'essential amino acids.'"

claims.claim_text: Are common calcium pills a good deal? Wallach says no - metallic mineral supplements like calcium carbonate are barely absorbed (about 8-12% in the young, falling to 3-5% after age 35-40). Worked example: a 1,000mg calcium carbonate tablet is only 400mg of actual (elemental) calcium, and at roughly a 10% absorption rate you net just ~80mg usable - so to truly get 2,000mg of usable calcium you'd have to swallow about 25 tablets a day (a 100-count bottle would last only 4 days). In his words: "Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day!"

He notes colloids keep their special qualities as long as the particles stay within a size range of about 1 to 100 nanometers - a range, he points out, known as 'nano-technology.' In his words: "The interesting thing about colloids is that they remain heterogeneous, multiphasic and insoluble at different concentrations as long as a larger number if not all of the particles are within a range of sizes of colloids (1nm to 100nm) known as 'nano-technology.'"

In his words: "In the presence of amino acids, a small percentage of the inorganic colloids form chelated minerals and organic colloids which are able to be dialyzed through the mucus membranes of the intestinal walls into the blood stream - this bio-available mineral state is known as a 'crystalloid.' Crystalloids or organic colloids readily pass through cell walls, while inorganic colloids are 'too large.'"

claims.claim_text: Aluminum is everywhere in the food supply, and Wallach frames that as normal, not alarming: it is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (about 12%) and is taken up by every plant grown in soil - so you cannot eat any grain, vegetable, fruit or nut, or drink any natural water, without ingesting it. He notes it is especially high in plankton and red algae and concentrates in mammals' hair and lungs. In his words: "Aluminum represents 12% of the earth's crust and is the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and the most abundant metal in the earth's crust."
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum represents 12%
of the earth’s crust and is the third most abundant element in the
earth’s crust and the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust.

claims.claim_text: Does aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease? Wallach says no - and calls the scare a myth built on 'a single faulty study.' He cites the follow-up work: a 1992 study in Nature by Frank Watt and colleagues at Oxford, using a highly accurate technique, found the same aluminum levels in the brains of non-Alzheimer's controls as in Alzheimer's patients; a 1997 Berkeley newsletter and a 2007 German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment opinion both concluded there is no proven link between dietary aluminum and Alzheimer's. In his words: "A single faulty study over 35 years ago suggested a link between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer's disease."
claims.verbatim:
A single faulty study over 35 years ago suggested a link
between chronic aluminum exposure and Alzheimer’s disease.

claims.claim_text: Actinium is a naturally occurring (and radioactive) element that Wallach includes among those detected in living tissue. Beyond the physics - it is a metal that, like radium, glows in the dark, and its name comes from the Greek aktinos ('ray') - his biological note is speculative but intriguing: actinium accumulates in the bones and liver, where he suggests it may have some metabolic function. He also observes that plant roots readily absorb it, though little travels up into the plant. Presented for the curious; Wallach assigns it no specific health role. In his words: "Actinium accumulates in and presumably has metabolic functions in the bones and liver."
claims.verbatim:
Actinium accumulates in and presumably has metabolic
functions in the bones and liver.

claims.claim_text: Arsenic - yes, the infamous poison - is, in the right trace amounts, an essential nutrient in Wallach's framework, recognized as such since 1947. He notes it normally circulates in human blood (rising during menstruation and pregnancy), that trace amounts stimulate red-blood-cell production and speed growth in young animals, and that (paired with the B-vitamin choline) it fully prevents a tendon disorder in poultry - a reminder that the dose which heals sits far below the dose that harms. In his words: "Arsenic was determined to be an essential nutrient in 1947; the French Academy first identified arsenic in dead human bodies in 1834."
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic was determined to be an essential nutrient
in 1947; the French Academy first identified arsenic in
dead human bodies in 1834.

claims.claim_text: A surprising deficiency link from Wallach: too little arsenic can surface as carpal tunnel syndrome, TMJ (temporomandibular joint, or jaw-joint, disorder), and other 'repetitive motion' type degenerative joint diseases - problems usually blamed on overuse rather than nutrition. He adds that trace amounts stimulate red-blood-cell production. In his words: "Arsenic deficiency in humans results in a 'carpal tunnel syndrome,' 'TMJ,' and other 'repetitive motion' type degenerative joint diseases and minute traces stimulate the production of red blood cells."
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic
deficiency in humans results in a “carpal tunnel syndrome,”
“TMJ,” and other “repetitive motion” type degenerative joint
diseases and minute traces stimulate the production of red
blood cells.

claims.claim_text: Arsenic isn't merely tolerated by the body - Wallach cites it as a leukemia treatment. Per the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, arsenic infusions work better than any other drug for certain leukemias; in a study of 12 gravely ill patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), 11 went into remission within 12-39 days, and 8 were still in remission ten years later - results the lead researcher said appeared to exceed any single drug for APL. In his words: "According to the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in New York, 'infusions of arsenic works better than any other drug for the treatment of certain types of leukemia.' Their study involved 12 seriously ill patients suffering from acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)."
claims.verbatim:
According to the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer

claims.claim_text: Gold is one of the 60 minerals Wallach counts as essential, and the biological clue he points to is where and how the body holds it: in the mammalian liver, gold occurs as a colloid - the same ultra-fine, absorbable particle state his framework says the body actually uses minerals in (as opposed to un-absorbable 'metallic' gold). He also notes gold concentrates in the horsetail plant (Equisetum arvense). Importantly, in this passage he documents gold's presence and colloidal form in the body rather than naming a specific gold-deficiency disease - so it is evidence that gold belongs among the essential, tissue-resident elements, not a stated function. In his words: "...in mammalian liver gold forms a colloid."

marine animals at 0.0003 to 0.008 ppm, terrestrial
animals at 0.00023 ppm, and in mammalian liver gold forms a

claims.claim_text: Does gold treat arthritis? Wallach's take is more cautionary than the mainstream - he is refining a common stance, not endorsing it. He acknowledges that orthodox physicians do give gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, aurothioglucose) as an add-on to aspirin for arthritis pain, but immediately qualifies it: gold has been reported effective ONLY against active joint inflammation, and is not usually helpful for advanced, destructive rheumatoid arthritis. So he is describing and limiting an existing orthodox therapy, not putting gold forward as a broad arthritis cure. In his words: "Gold compounds ... are frequently administered by orthodox physicians as an add-on therapy with salicylates (aspirin) for arthritis when added pain relief is required. Gold has been reported only to be effective against active joint inflammation and is not usually helpful for treating advanced destructive rheumatoid arthritis."
claims.verbatim:
Gold compounds (gold sodium thiomalate, gold
thioglucose also known as aurothioglucose) are frequently
administered by orthodox physicians as an add-on therapy
with salicylates (aspirin) for arthritis when added pain relief
is required. Gold has been reported only to be effective
against active joint inflammation and is not usually helpful
for treating advanced destructive rheumatoid arthritis.

claims.claim_text: Separate from gold's nutritional role, Wallach notes a purely medical use of a radioactive form of gold: gold-198, a short-lived isotope (half-life 2.7 days, made by bombarding natural gold with neutrons in a reactor), is used to treat some forms of cancer. This is radiation therapy, not nutrition - included for reference. In his words: "A radioactive isotope of gold with a short half-life of 2.7 days is used to treat some forms of cancer. Known as gold-198, it is easily produced by exposing natural gold to a beam of neutrons in a nuclear reactor."
claims.verbatim:
A radioactive isotope of gold
with a short half-life of 2.7 days is used to treat some forms of
cancer. Known as gold-198, it is easily produced by exposing
natural gold to a beam of neutrons in a nuclear reactor.

claims.claim_text: Boron is one of the 60 minerals Wallach counts as essential - though mainstream science was slow to agree, accepting it as an essential nutrient for humans only in 1990 (it had been shown essential for growing chicks about a decade earlier). Its core job, per Wallach, is in bone metabolism: it helps the body use calcium and magnesium efficiently and keeps the endocrine glands - the hormone-producing ovaries, testes and adrenals - working properly. In his words: "Boron is essential for bone metabolism including the efficient use of calcium and magnesium and proper function of endocrine glands (i.e. - ovaries, testes and adrenals)."
claims.verbatim:
Boron is essential for bone metabolism including the
efficient use of calcium and magnesium and proper function
of endocrine glands (i.e. - ovaries, testes and adrenals).

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to boron's bone-protective and hormonal effects. He says it is needed both to maintain bone density and to keep normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. He cites a supplementation finding: within eight days of taking boron, women held on to far more of their minerals - excreting 40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus in their urine - while their level of 17-beta estradiol (the main, most active form of estrogen) doubled to what is seen in women on estrogen-replacement therapy, and testosterone doubled in both men and women. In his words: "Boron is required for the maintenance of bone density and normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. Within eight days of supplementing boron, women lost 40% less calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus through their urine. Women receiving boron supplements had blood levels of estradiol 17B doubled to 'levels found in women on estrogen replacement therapy.' Levels of testosterone also double in both men and women following boron supplementation."

Boron is required for the maintenance of bone density
and normal blood levels of estrogen and testosterone. Within
eight days of supplementing boron, women lost 40% less
calcium, 33% less magnesium, and less phosphorus through
their urine. Women receiving boron supplements had blood
levels of estradiol 17B doubled to “levels found in women
on estrogen replacement therapy.” Levels of testosterone
also double in both men and women following boron
supplementation.

claims.claim_text: Barium is one of the 60 minerals Wallach counts as essential (recognized as essential for mammals in 1949). To most people, though, barium is familiar from medicine: because barium sulfate is a very dense salt that blocks X-rays, radiologists have a patient drink it (a 'barium swallow') or receive it as an enema so the hollow organs of the digestive tract show up clearly, outlined in white, on the film. In his words: "As the barium sulfate absorbs X-rays and blocks their transmission, the gastrointestinal organs will be clearly outlined in white in an X-ray film. Barium was considered essential for mammals in 1949."
claims.verbatim:
As the barium
sulfate absorbs X-rays and blocks their transmission, the
gastrointestinal organs will be clearly outlined in white in an
X-ray film.

Barium was considered essential for mammals in 1949.

claims.claim_text: Beryllium is on Wallach's list of essential minerals, but it is one of the thin ones - in this book he assigns it no specific positive role in the body, offering mostly geology and history (it heads the 'alkaline-earth' metal family, alongside calcium and magnesium). What he does flag is a hazard: breathing beryllium-oxide dust, a mining and industrial contaminant, can cause berylliosis, a painful and sometimes fatal lung disease. In his words: "Inhalation of beryllium oxide dust (mining and industrial contaminants) can lead to “berylliosis,” a painful and sometimes fatal lung disease."
claims.verbatim:
Inhalation of beryllium oxide dust (mining and
industrial contaminants) can lead to “berylliosis,” a painful

claims.claim_text: Bismuth is not one of Wallach's essential nutrients, but he gives it a memorable entry. Chinese physicians used it for stomach ulcers and gut infections for thousands of years, and today it is the pink liquid in over-the-counter remedies like Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate). His larger point is a myth-buster: stress was blamed for decades as the cause of gastric, peptic and duodenal ulcers, but the real cause turned out to be infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori - a link Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed in 1983 (and one already known in pigs back in 1952). The standard treatment pairs antibiotics and antacids with bismuth subsalicylate. In his words: "Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as Helicobacter pylori. Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D. and pathologist J. Robin Warren proposed their theory for the bacterial cause of gastric ulcers in 1983. The bacterial cause (H. pylori) for gastric ulcers was known in pigs in 1952."
claims.verbatim:
Stress has historically been blamed as the boogy-man
as the cause of gastric, peptic, and duodenal ulcers. Animal
and human studies have in fact demonstrated that the true
cause of ulcers is an infection with a bacterium known as
Helicobacter pylori.

Australian gastroenterologist Barry Marshall, M.D.

claims.claim_text: Bromine is a canon essential mineral in Wallach's framework and a halogen - the same chemical family as iodine. He says it works in the body in its active form as brominated amino acids, and that there is strong evidence for its essentiality in both mammals and humans. In his words: "There is strong evidence for Bromine's essentiality in mammals and humans."
claims.verbatim:
There is strong evidence for Bromine’s essentiality in
mammals and humans.

claims.claim_text: A bit of history on bromine: sodium bromide (a bromine salt) was a common mild sedative in the late 1800s and early 1900s, prescribed to calm the nerves. That is where the old expression comes from - people still talk about taking a 'bromide' to settle down and ease stress and tension. In his words: "Sodium bromide, a salt of bromine, is a mild sedative that was commonly used in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. People still speak of taking a “bromide” to calm down and ease stress and tension."
claims.verbatim:
Sodium bromide, a salt of bromine, is a mild sedative
that was commonly used in the late 19th and early 20th
centuries. People still speak of taking a “bromide” to calm

claims.claim_text: Carbon is the element most essential for life on Earth - Wallach calls it the center of the 'organic' world. Because carbon atoms link into long chains that form the backbone (spine) of almost every biological molecule, virtually all of the body's building blocks are carbon-based: carbohydrates, fats, amino acids, vitamins and enzymes. DNA itself is one such long carbon-chain molecule. In his words: "Carbon functions as an essential structural element for all living organisms and organic molecules (i.e.- carbohydrates, fats, amino acids, vitamins, enzymes, etc.)."
claims.verbatim:
Carbon functions as an essential structural element for
all living organisms and organic molecules (i.e.- carbohydrates,
fats, amino acids, vitamins, enzymes, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Outside of nutrition, Wallach shares his personal view on climate. He is skeptical of blaming human activity for global warming - he calls humanity's share of the planet's biomass 'pitifully small' and argues that Ice Ages and warm periods have cycled naturally throughout Earth's history, so today's warming is part of that long-running cycle. His proposed remedy is simply to plant more trees, which pull carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen and water. (Recorded as his own stance on a debated, non-health topic, outside the book's nutrition framework.) In his words: "While many individuals and organizations, want to blame man's activities and pitifully small biomass for “global warming,” we must look to the past for the cycles of Ice Ages and “global warming” that have taken place over and over through the millennia to understand the cyclic nature of these events."
claims.verbatim:
While many individuals and organizations, want to
blame man’s activities and pitifully small biomass for “global
warming,” we must look to the past for the cycles of Ice Ages and
“global warming” that have taken place over and over through
the millennia to understand the cyclic nature of these events.

claims.claim_text: What are carbohydrates? Wallach explains that carbs and sugars are the body's convenient everyday fuel, but - importantly - they are NOT essential nutrients: the body can make all the carbohydrate it needs by reconfiguring proteins and fats. Plants build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight (photosynthesis, which runs on chlorophyll, a magnesium/carbon ring). Carbohydrates are classified by size: single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose and fructose), double sugars (disaccharides like sucrose, maltose and lactose), and large chains (polysaccharides like starch, cellulose, fiber and glycogen). In his words: "While carbohydrates and sugars are convenient sources of fuel for energy, they are not essential nutrients as all living organisms can make them by reconfiguring proteins and fats."
claims.verbatim:
While
carbohydrates and sugars are convenient sources of fuel for
energy, they are not essential nutrients as all living organisms
can make them by reconfiguring proteins and fats.

claims.claim_text: A primer on fats: like carbohydrates, fats (lipids) are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but they don't dissolve in water and pack more energy - about 9 calories per gram versus 4.5 for carbohydrate or protein. The main form of fat is the triglyceride: a molecule of glycerol joined to fatty acids. Fatty acids are described three ways - chain length (short, medium or long, by the number of carbons), how 'saturated' they are with hydrogen (no double bonds = saturated; one = monounsaturated; several = polyunsaturated), and where the first double bond sits counting from the tail (the 'omega' number, e.g. omega-3, omega-6). In his words: "Triglycerides (the primary component of fats and oils) are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Structurally, they are esters of a trihydric alcohol (glycerol) and fatty acids."
claims.verbatim:
Triglycerides (the primary component of fats and oils)
are composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Structurally,
they are esters of a trihydric alcohol (glycerol) and fatty acids.

claims.claim_text: Essential fatty acids (EFA) are the fats the body cannot make for itself and so must get from food. Wallach names three polyunsaturated ones - linoleic, linolenic and arachidonic acid - and notes only two (linoleic and linolenic) are strictly essential, since the body can build arachidonic acid from linolenic; about 3% of daily calories should come from EFAs. They do vitamin-like jobs: carrying and processing fat, keeping cell membranes intact, lowering blood cholesterol, and serving as the raw material for prostaglandins that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, blood clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function. A shortage is especially damaging in infants. In his words: "EFA deficiency in human infants results in a poor growth rate, lowered IQ, seizures, learning disabilities, eczema, asthma, and a lowered resistance to infectious diseases."
claims.verbatim:
EFA deficiency in human infants results in a poor growth rate,
lowered IQ, seizures, learning disabilities, eczema, asthma,
and a lowered resistance to infectious diseases.

claims.claim_text: Is cholesterol bad for you? Wallach's answer is emphatically no - it is essential. It is a structural part of every cell membrane and of the myelin that insulates the brain and spinal cord, and it is the raw material the body uses to make vitamin D, bile acids (which digest fat), the adrenal stress hormones, and the sex hormones estrogen, progesterone and testosterone. Because of that hormone role, he warns that a cholesterol deficiency can make menopause miserable and can flatten sex drive in both men and women. In his words: "Cholesterol is an essential part of the structure of cell walls, brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw material for the production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids, adrenal cortical hormones, estrogens (a cholesterol deficiency makes menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a cholesterol deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching steer who is totally disinterested in sex)."
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part of the structure of cell walls,
brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw material for the
production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids, adrenal
cortical hormones, estrogens (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone (a
cholesterol deficiency will turn hubby into a TV watching
steer who is totally disinterested in sex).

claims.claim_text: What are proteins? Like carbohydrates and fats they contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but proteins add nitrogen (about 16%, the 'amine' group), sometimes with phosphorus, iron, sulfur or cobalt. Their basic building block is the amino acid; amino acids link by 'peptide bonds' into long chains, and digestion breaks those bonds to free the individual amino acids again. Proteins are the most abundant carbon-based compound in the body - the main stuff of muscle and every cell - and enzymes (the workers that speed up the body's chemical reactions) are themselves proteins. In his words: "Proteins are the fundamental structural components of the living cell (cytoplasm). They are essential parts of the cell nucleus and protoplasm. Proteins are the most abundant of all carbon containing organic compounds in the human body."
claims.verbatim:
Proteins are the fundamental structural components
of the living cell (cytoplasm). They are essential parts of the
cell nucleus and protoplasm. Proteins are the most abundant
of all carbon containing organic compounds in the human
body.

claims.claim_text: Can you eat too much protein? Wallach's view: a healthy person can consume even 300 grams of protein a day - nearly three-quarters of a pound of meat - with no ill effects, as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and they supplement properly with vitamins and minerals. In his words: "An individual consuming protein at even 300 gm per day (almost 3/4 of a pound of meat a day) will have no adverse effects as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and supplement properly with vitamins and minerals."
claims.verbatim:
An individual consuming protein at even 300 gm per
day (almost 3/4 of a pound of meat a day) will have no adverse
effects as long as they do not have kidney or liver disease and
supplement properly with vitamins and minerals.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's essential amino acids and what each does. Classically there are nine that must come from the diet because the body cannot make them, and Wallach would add three more - arginine, taurine and tyrosine. Their roles: valine, lysine, threonine, leucine and isoleucine build protein; tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin; phenylalanine makes thyroxine (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); methionine makes choline and creatine phosphate; histidine makes histamine; and the added three help prevent specific diseases (arginine, taurine, tyrosine - see the related claim). In his words: "Classically there are nine essential amino acids that are required in the daily diet as they cannot be manufactured by the human body."
claims.verbatim:
Classically there are nine essential amino acids that are
required in the daily diet as they cannot be manufactured by
the human body.

claims.claim_text: Beyond the classic list, Wallach singles out three amino acids that, over the long haul, help prevent specific diseases: arginine guards against cancer and PAD (peripheral arterial disease, clogged arteries in the limbs), taurine against macular degeneration (an eye disease that erodes central vision), and tyrosine against goiter (a swollen thyroid). In his words: "To the classic list of essential amino acids, we would add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases, respectively, these diseases are cancer and PAD, macular degeneration and goiter."
claims.verbatim:
To the classic list of essential amino acids, we would
add arginine, taurine, and tyrosine. Over the long haul, these
three amino acids help prevent certain specific diseases,

degeneration and goiter.

claims.claim_text: What are vitamins? Wallach defines them as a group of unrelated, carbon-based organic compounds the body needs in tiny daily amounts for specific chemical reactions - essential for normal growth, development, maintenance, health, longevity and life itself. They work mainly as coenzymes (helper molecules that switch enzymes on) and cannot be manufactured by the human body, yet they supply no calories and add no body mass. Getting optimal vitamins, he says, goes a long way toward preventing birth defects and many debilitating degenerative diseases. In his words: "Vitamins are essential nutrients in that, they can not be manufactured by humans; they do not supply calories or contribute to body mass."
claims.verbatim:
Vitamins are essential nutrients in that, they can not
be manufactured by humans; they do not supply calories or
contribute to body mass.

claims.claim_text: Wallach sorts vitamins into three classes. (1) Fat-soluble - A, D, E and K - work in fat metabolism and cannot be absorbed on a very low-fat diet; people who have had their gallbladder removed should take ox bile to supply the bile salts needed to absorb fats and fat-soluble vitamins. (2) Water-soluble - the ten B vitamins plus vitamin C - act as cofactors that help cells turn food into energy. (3) Flavanols - the bioflavonoids (polyphenols / epicatechins) - which he counts as a third vitamin category. Flavanols in dark chocolate, he notes, help keep capillaries strong, lower blood pressure and improve blood flow. In his words: "Flavanols found in dark chocolate, participate in maintaining the strength of capillaries, lower blood pressure, improve blood flow via increased production of nitric oxide (a molecule used by the vascular endothelium to signal the surrounding muscle to relax) and have vitamin C-like functions."

claims.claim_text: Calcium is essential for all living organisms — it forms the cell walls of plants, all calcareous tissues, and mammalian bones and teeth. Beyond that structural role, it also helps regulate the electrochemical functions inside cells and is a required cofactor that activates several enzymes. It is the fifth most abundant mineral element in the earth's crust and biosphere. In his words: "Calcium is essential for all living organisms and is found in the cell walls of plants, in all calcareous tissues, and mammalian bones and teeth. Calcium also helps to regulate electrochemical functions in cells and is a required cofactor necessary to activate several enzymes."

Calcium is essential for all living organisms and is

claims.claim_text: Wallach argues humans are biologically designed to eat high-calcium diets. In the late Paleolithic (35,000–10,000 years ago), wild plant foods and game supplied about 1,600 mg of calcium a day at rest and 2,000–3,000 mg at the activity levels of hunting and labor. The agricultural revolution ~10,000 years ago narrowed the variety of foods and permanently lowered mineral intake — by the 20th century American adults took in only one-fifth to one-third as much, a median of 300–508 mg/day for women and 680 mg/day for men (National Health & Nutrition Examination Survey II). In his words: "The uncultivated food plants and wild game commonly available to Stone Age humans would supply 1600 mg of calcium at basal energy intakes and between 2,000 and 3,000 mg of calcium at the energy levels required to support hunting and work."

The average man holds about 1,200 grams and the average woman about 1,000 grams — roughly 2% of adult body weight, and up to 39% of the body's total mineral reserves (the ash left after cremation). adult body weight (water makes up 65 to 75%). Calcium also

cremation). Ninety-nine percent of body calcium is found in
bones and teeth. The other one percent is found in the blood,
extracellular fluids, and within cells where it is a cofactor and
activator for numerous enzyme systems.

In his words: "in a classic crystal structure bound to a protein framework called “bone matrix.” To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the protein matrix, put a chicken “drumstick” bone in a quart of vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of the bone leaving the protein matrix."

claims.claim_text: Beyond its structural role, calcium is a working cofactor throughout the body. Calcium also governs transport across cell and organelle membranes, the release of neurotransmitters at synapses, the secretion and effects of hormones and enzymes, and the rate and strength of the heartbeat, muscle tone and nerve responsiveness. In his words: "In addition to being a major structural mineral, Ca is also required as a cofactor for the release of energy from ATP for muscular contraction, and blood clotting. In the blood clotting process, ionized Ca stimulates the release of thromboplastin from platelets and converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin helps to convert fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin is the protein web that traps red blood cells to create blood clots."

claims.claim_text: How well calcium is absorbed depends heavily on its form and the gut environment. Wallach lists the causes of a calcium deficiency as: too little vitamin D; low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, which can follow a salt-restricted diet); lactose intolerance; celiac disease; a high-fat or low-protein diet; and heavy fiber and phytate intake. Phytic acid (in grain bran, oatmeal, whole wheat) and oxalic acid (in rhubarb, spinach, chard, mustard greens) each bind calcium into insoluble, unabsorbable salts, and excess sugar, carbonation and caffeine leach stored calcium from the bones. In his words: "Causes of a calcium deficiency can include, a deficiency or lack of vitamin D; the lack of stomach acid or hypochlorhydria can result from a restricted NaCl (salt) intake; lactose intolerance; celiac disease; high fat diet; low protein diet; and a high fiber and phytate consumption."

claims.claim_text: The body holds blood calcium within a tight range using two hormones. by 33.3%, when they were supplemented, with chromium.
Prior to this study, gerontologist, led by Dr. Roy Walford,
felt a Calorie Restricted diet was the only way to extend life
past the expected average age. Deficiencies of chromium in
humans are characterized by a wide variety of clinical diseases
as well as a shortened life expectancy. The clinical diseases of
chromium deficiency are aggravated by concurrent vanadium
deficiencies and increased sugar or alcohol intakes.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains why chromium is both easy to lose and hard to absorb — his argument for supplementing it in a highly-absorbable form. Eating sugar (colas, fruit juices, honey, candy, table sugar, fructose) raises the rate at which chromium is flushed out in the urine by 300% for 12 hours. And ordinary inorganic chromium from food and water is poorly used: a typical 50-100 microgram (mcg) intake yields only 0.25-5 mcg the body can actually retain. Form is decisive — about 25% of chelated chromium is absorbed, versus up to 98% of colloidal chromium. He notes the chromium RDA (the government's Recommended Daily Allowance) is 50-200 mcg of usable chromium per day for adults. In his words: "...25% of chelated chromium is absorbed and up to 98% of colloidal chromium is absorbed. The chromium RDA for humans is a range of 50 to 200 ug of usable chromium per day for adults."

Dietary sugar
loads (i.e. colas, apple juice, grape juice, honey, candy, table
sugar, fructose, etc.) increase the natural rate of urinary Cr loss
by 300% for 12 hours. The average intake of 50 to 100 ug of
inorganic chromium from food and water supplies only 0.25
to 5 ug of usable and retainable chromium. By contrast, 25%
of chelated chromium is absorbed and up to 98% of colloidal


 

chromium is absorbed. The chromium RDA for humans is a
range of 50 to 200 ug of usable chromium per day for adults.

claims.claim_text: A recurring worry in the book: Americans' chromium status has been sliding for decades. Newborn animals and people carry more chromium per pound of body weight than older ones, and in anyone who doesn't supplement, tissue chromium steadily falls with age. Wallach flags a population-wide drop in average American blood chromium since 1948, tabulating mean levels in micrograms per liter (mcg/L) by year: 28 in cities and 1000 in rural areas in 1948, 13 in 1971, 10 in 1972, 4.7-5.1 in 1973, 0.73-1.6 in 1974, 0.16 in 1978, 0.43 in 1980, and 0.13 by 1985. In his words: "The concentration of chromium found in newborn animals and humans is higher per pound of body weight than it is in older individuals... Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the average American serum chromium since 1948."

animals and humans is higher per pound of body weight
than it is in older individuals. In fact, the chromium levels of

claims.claim_text: The element's backstory — and why it colors gemstones. Chromium was discovered by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek chroma, 'color,' because all its compounds are vividly colored (the pure metal itself, though, is a hard, brittle, silver-white). Added to steel at 18% it makes stainless steel, and its near-invisible corrosion-proof oxide layer makes it the bright plating on bathroom fixtures, jewelry and car bumpers. Trace chromium is what tints many gems: it makes rubies red (in corundum), emeralds green (in beryl), and gives alexandrite (in chrysoberyl) its famous color-shift — red in firelight, blue in daylight. In his words: "Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek word chroma, which translates to 'color.'"
claims.verbatim:
Chromium was discovered by French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin in 1797 and named from the Greek word
chroma, which translates to “color.”

claims.claim_text: Cesium is an alkali (alkaline) metal, so chemically it behaves much like sodium, potassium and rubidium. Wallach describes cesium and potassium forming a 'solute complex' inside the cell that takes part in ion antagonism (the balancing push-pull between minerals), osmosis, regulating what crosses the cell membrane (permeability), and keeping the cell's interior in its proper gel-like 'colloidal' state. Because the two minerals trade places, taking extra potassium speeds up how fast the body excretes and loses cesium. In his words: "As an alkaline mineral, cesium behaves chemically in a similar manner as sodium, potassium and rubidium. Cesium and potassium enter into a solute complex, which participates in ion antagonism, osmosis, permeability regulation, and maintenance of the colloidal state in the living cell. The increase in supplemental potassium increases the rate of excretion or loss of cesium."
claims.verbatim:
As an alkaline mineral, cesium behaves chemically in a
similar manner as sodium, potassium and rubidium. Cesium
and potassium enter into a solute complex, which participates
in ion antagonism, osmosis, permeability regulation, and
maintenance of the colloidal state in the living cell. The increase
in supplemental potassium increases the rate of excretion or
loss of cesium.

claims.claim_text: The element's discovery story. Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, who identified it by its spectral 'fingerprint' — the specific colors of light (spectral emission lines) it emits when heated. Those lines were a bright sky-blue, which is why they named it cesium, from the Latin caesius ('sky blue'). In his words: "Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. They isolated cesium by observing colors or spectral emission lines, that cesium emits when it is heated. The color lines were bright blue, which prompted them to name the element cesium after the Latin coesius ('sky blue')."
claims.verbatim:
Cesium was discovered in 1860 by the German chemists
Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. They isolated cesium by
observing colors or spectral emission lines, that cesium emits
when it is heated. The color lines were bright blue, which
prompted them to name the element cesium after the Latin
coesius (“sky blue”).

claims.claim_text: Wallach presents cesium chloride as a cancer therapy — the basis of what's called 'high-pH therapy.' The idea: cesium enters the cancer cell and makes its interior alkaline (raises its pH), an environment hostile to the cancer. He says it has been recommended for all cancers, including sarcomas (cancers of connective or soft tissue), bronchiogenic carcinoma (lung cancer arising in the bronchi), and colon cancer. In his words: "Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer therapy programs. Cesium provides 'high pH therapy' for cancer by entering the cancer cell and producing an alkaline environment. It has been recommended for all cancers including sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma and colon cancer."
claims.verbatim:
Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer
therapy programs. Cesium provides “high pH therapy” for
cancer by entering the cancer cell and producing an alkaline
environment. It has been recommended for all cancers including
sarcomas, bronchiogenic carcinoma and colon cancer.

claims.claim_text: The element's name and history. Copper makes up only 0.007% of the earth's crust. Its name comes from the Latin cuprum, meaning 'from Cyprus' — the Romans mined their copper on the island of Cyprus. Copper was one of the first metals humanity used: copper jewelry from about 9000 B.C. has been found in Iraq. Because pure copper is soft, ancient peoples alloyed it with tin to make bronze, zinc to make brass, and nickel to make monel, producing harder metals for tools and weapons. In his words: "Despite the common use of copper, it makes up only 0.007% of the earth's crust. Copper gets its name from the Latin word, cuprum, which translates to 'from Cyprus,' a reference to the fact that the Romans mined their copper from the island of Cyprus."
claims.verbatim:
Despite the common use of copper, it makes up only
0.007% of the earth’s crust. Copper gets its name from the
Latin word, cuprum, which translates to “from Cyprus,” a
reference to the fact that the Romans mined their copper from
the island of Cyprus.

claims.claim_text: Copper is a genuine essential nutrient for every living thing. Wallach frames it as a universally important cofactor — a helper the body's enzymes need to work — for many hundreds of metalloenzymes (enzymes built around a metal atom). He stresses that copper deficiency is widespread and common, and that copper-deficiency diseases have a real impact on human populations. In his words: "Copper is an essential nutrient for all living organisms and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and common and copper deficiency diseases have an important impact on human populations."
claims.verbatim:
Copper is an essential nutrient for all living organisms
and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds
of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and
common and copper deficiency diseases have an important
impact on human populations.

claims.claim_text: Wallach prints a long table of the conditions he attributes to copper deficiency — many tied to copper's role in pigment, connective tissue and blood vessels. Hair and skin: white/grey/'silver' hair, vitiligo (loss of skin pigment), dry brittle hair. Sagging and weakened tissue: ptosis (drooping eyelids, 'crow's feet,' sagging skin/breasts/belly), hernias, varicose veins, hemorrhoids, spider veins, and aneurysms (rupture-prone weak spots in artery walls) — including Kawasaki disease (childhood aneurysms with streptococcal infection). Also anemia, hypo- and hyperthyroid dysfunction, arthritis, disc disease and liver cirrhosis. Neuro-behavioral: violent behavior / blind rage / 'criminal' behavior, learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some autism), cerebral palsy, and aplasia/hypoplasia (underdevelopment) of the cerebellum. Copper-deficiency brain diseases across species: enzootic ataxia in sheep, Mad Cow Disease in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. Plus elevated blood cholesterol (above 350), iron storage disease (hemosiderosis), reduced carbohydrate tolerance, and neutropenia (low neutrophil count). In his words: "Copper deficiency Symptoms and Diseases: White, grey and 'silver' hair; Vitiligo; Dry brittle hair; Ptosis; Hernias; Varicose veins (including hemorrhoids); Spider veins; Aneurysms; Kawasaki disease; Anemia; Hypo and hyperthyroid dysfunction; Arthritis; Disc disease; Liver cirrhosis; Violent behavior, blind rage, explosive outbursts and 'criminal' behavior; Learning disabilities (ADD, ADHD, some forms of autism); Cerebral palsy, aplasia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum; Enzootic ataxia in sheep; Mad Cow Disease in cattle; Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease; Elevated blood cholesterol (above 350); Iron storage disease (hemosiderosis); Reduced carbohydrate tolerance; Neutropenia."

claims.claim_text: Wallach lists the many jobs copper does inside cells and tissues. It's needed for RNA and DNA; for lysyl oxidase, the copper enzyme that cross-links and strengthens elastic fibers; for making melanin (the pigment of skin and hair); and for electron transport, the cell's energy-generating respiration chain. Through those elastic fibers copper gives tensile strength to skin, hair, wool (poor copper makes 'steely wool' in sheep), cartilage, tendons, ligaments, the vertebral discs and blood vessels. In his words: "Copper is required for many subcellular and physiological functions: RNA, DNA, Lysyl oxidase (elastic fiber cofactor), melanin production (skin and hair), electron transport for subcellular respiration, tensile strength of elastic fibers in skin, hair, wool ('steely wool'), cartilage, tendons, ligaments, vertebral discs, blood vessels, etc."
claims.verbatim:
Copper is required for many subcellular and
physiological functions: RNA, DNA, Lysyl oxidase (elastic
fiber cofactor), melanin production (skin and hair), electron
transport for subcellular respiration, tensile strength of elastic
fibers in skin, hair, wool (“steely wool”), cartilage, tendons,
ligaments, vertebral discs, blood vessels, etc.

claims.claim_text: One of the earliest proofs that copper deficiency causes neurological disease. In 1937, 'enzootic ataxia' in newborn lambs — also called sway back or lamkruis, a loss of muscle coordination — was recognized as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep. Giving the ewes copper supplements prevented it. The disease was marked by demyelination (loss of the protective myelin sheath around nerves) in the cerebellum (the brain's coordination center) and the spinal cord. In his words: "Neonatal 'enzootic ataxia' (sway back, lamkruis) was recognized as a clinical and disease entity in 1937 as a copper deficiency in pregnant sheep. Copper supplements prevented the syndrome, which was characterized by demyelination of the cerebellum and spinal cord."
claims.verbatim:
Neonatal “enzootic ataxia” (sway back, lamkruis) was
recognized as a clinical and disease entity in 1937 as a copper
deficiency in pregnant sheep. Copper supplements prevented
the syndrome, which was characterized by demyelination of
the cerebellum and spinal cord.

claims.claim_text: Wallach classifies Mad Cow Disease — technically Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) — and its human counterpart, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, as copper-deficiency diseases. His evidence is the brain damage itself: the lesions of BSE closely resemble those of enzootic ataxia in sheep, a long-established copper-deficiency disease. In his words: "The brain lesions of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) appear to be similar to those of Enzootic Ataxia in sheep - a copper deficiency."
claims.verbatim:
The brain lesions of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy
(BSE) appear to be similar to those of Enzootic Ataxia in sheep
- a copper deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Wallach extends the copper-deficiency argument to cerebral palsy. In sheep, copper deficiency produces a set of brain lesions — cavities or jelly-like damage in the cerebral white matter, chromatolysis (breakdown of nerve-cell structures), nerve-cell death, and myelin aplasia (myelin failing to form during fetal development). He says these congenital lesions are identical to the classic brain changes of human cerebral palsy. In his words: "Cavitation or gelatinous lesions of the cerebral white matter, chromatolysis, nerve cell death and myelin aplasia (failure to form during embryonic development) were also identified as a copper deficiency disease in sheep - these congenital lesions are identical to those of the classical changes of human cerebral palsy."
claims.verbatim:
Cavitation or gelatinous lesions of the cerebral white
matter, chromatolysis, nerve cell death and myelin aplasia
(failure to form during embryonic development) were also
identified as a copper deficiency disease in sheep - these
congenital lesions are identical to those of the classical changes
of human cerebral palsy.

claims.claim_text: To dramatize how common copper deficiency is, Wallach names famous people he says show its signs — mostly fatal aneurysms (weak arterial walls that balloon and burst, an elastin failure copper is meant to prevent): Albert Einstein (ruptured aortic aneurysm), Franklin D. Roosevelt (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), the nutritionist Paavo Airola (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Conway Twitty and John Ritter (ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms), and George and Barbara Bush (thyroid disease and white hair). He adds a striking autopsy statistic: 4 to 6 of every 100 Americans autopsied died of a ruptured aneurysm, and another 40% had aneurysms that had not yet ruptured. In his words: "Famous people affected or dying of an obvious copper deficiency include: Albert Einstein (ruptured aortic aneurysm), Franklin D. Roosevelt (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Paavo Airola (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Conway Twitty (ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm), John Ritter (ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm), George and Barbara Bush (thyroid disease and white hair). Four to six out of every 100 Americans autopsied have died of a ruptured aneurysm; an additional 40% of Americans autopsied have aneurysms that have not ruptured."

deficiency include: Albert Einstein (ruptured aortic aneurysm),
Franklin D. Roosevelt (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Paavo
Airola (ruptured cerebral aneurysm), Conway Twitty
(ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm), John Ritter (ruptured
abdominal aortic aneurysm), George and Barbara Bush
(thyroid disease and white hair). Four to six out of every 100

additional 40% of Americans autopsied have aneurysms that


 

have not ruptured.

claims.claim_text: Wallach gives the body's copper content and daily needs. A well-nourished adult holds about 80–120 mg of copper total, concentrated in the brain, liver, heart and kidneys; bone and muscle hold lower percentages but, by sheer mass, store about half the body's copper. Newborns carry the highest concentrations. The daily copper requirement is highest per unit of body weight in the newborn — 0.08 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) — dropping to 0.04 mg/kg for toddlers and just 0.03 mg/kg for adults. In his words: "The daily copper requirement for the newborn is 0.08 mg/kg; toddlers require 0.04 mg/kg; and adults only 0.03 mg/kg."
claims.verbatim:
The daily copper requirement for the newborn is 0.08
mg/kg; toddlers require 0.04 mg/kg; and adults only 0.03
mg/kg.

claims.claim_text: Typical copper levels in the blood. Wallach gives average plasma copper as 87–153 (women) and 89–137 (men) — the book prints the unit as mg/dl, but for copper this is really micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL), the standard unit for plasma copper. About 90% of the copper in plasma travels bound to a carrier protein called ceruloplasmin. In his words: "The average plasma copper levels of women ranges from 87 to 153 mg/dl; for men the range is 89 to 137 mg/dl. About 90% of the plasma copper is bound in a protein called ceruloplasmin."
claims.verbatim:
The average plasma copper levels of women ranges
from 87 to 153 mg/dl; for men the range is 89 to 137 mg/dl.
About 90% of the plasma copper is bound in a protein called
ceruloplasmin.

claims.claim_text: The mechanism behind copper's cardiovascular effects. Copper activates numerous 'cupro-enzymes' (copper-dependent enzymes) that build and maintain the heart and blood vessels. In a copper-deficient pregnancy this causes congenital defects of the heart and vessels (Kawasaki disease) and of the brain (cerebral palsy, plus atresia — failure to form — and hypoplasia, or underdevelopment, of the cerebellum). Copper deficiency also lowers the activity of lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that converts proelastin into elastin; with less elastin, the walls of veins and arteries lose tensile strength — producing spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms. In his words: "Copper functions as a cofactor and activator of numerous cupro-enzymes that are involved with the development and maintenance of the cardiovascular system. Deficiency of copper in the pregnant female results in congenital defects of the heart and vascular system (Kawasaki disease) and brain (cerebral palsy, atresia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum). Deficiency of copper also results in reduced lysyl oxidase activity causing a reduction in conversion of proelastin to elastin causing a decrease in the tensile strength of venous and arterial walls (spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids and aneurysms)."
claims.verbatim:
Copper functions as a cofactor and activator of numerous
cupro-enzymes that are involved with the development and
maintenance of the cardiovascular system. Deficiency of
copper in the pregnant female results in congenital defects of
the heart and vascular system (Kawasaki disease) and brain
(cerebral palsy, atresia and hypoplasia of the cerebellum).
Deficiency of copper also results in reduced lysyl oxidase
activity causing a reduction in conversion of proelastin to
elastin causing a decrease in the tensile strength of venous
and arterial walls (spider veins, varicose veins, hemorrhoids
and aneurysms).

claims.claim_text: Copper deficiency also weakens the body's structural framework — bone, connective tissue and muscle. Wallach says this can produce a specific childhood arthritis that forms bone spurs (bony overgrowths) in the growth plates, the zones of developing cartilage at the ends of a child's bones. In his words: "Deficiency of copper also results in a reduced skeletal, connective tissue and muscular integrity which can produce a specific type of arthritis in children that forms bone spurs in the bone growth plates."
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency of copper also results in a reduced skeletal,
connective tissue and muscular integrity which can produce
a specific type of arthritis in children that forms bone spurs in
the bone growth plates.

claims.claim_text: The earliest and most telling signs of copper deficiency, especially in infants. Too little copper causes myelin defects (poor nerve insulation), anemia, poorly-formed ('keratinized') hair, and loss of hair color. In a baby, the earliest laboratory signs are neutropenia (too few neutrophils, a type of white blood cell) and leukopenia (a low total white-cell count). Infants fed mainly cow's milk — which is low in copper — often develop copper-deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease. In his words: "Lack of copper can result in myelin defects, anemia, poor hair keratinization and loss of hair color. Neutropenia (reduced numbers of neutrophilic WBCs or white blood cells) and leucopenia (reduced total WBC count) are the earliest indications of a copper deficiency in an infant. Infants whose diets are primarily cow's milk frequently develop copper deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease."
claims.verbatim:
Lack of copper can result in myelin defects, anemia,
poor hair keratinization and loss of hair color. Neutropenia
(reduced numbers of neutrophilic WBCs or white blood cells)
and leucopenia (reduced total WBC count) are the earliest
indications of a copper deficiency in an infant. Infants whose
diets are primarily cow’s milk frequently develop copper
deficiency anemia and/or iron storage disease.

claims.claim_text: Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome is the clearest genetic proof of copper's importance. Wallach describes it as a sex-linked recessive genetic defect (carried on the X chromosome) that blocks copper absorption. Affected infants show stunted growth, defective keratin in the hair (the 'kinky' hair), loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (from low thyroid function) and anemia, degeneration and fractures of the aortic elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of the long bones, and progressive mental deterioration — the last because the brain is left without cytochrome oxidase, a vital copper-dependent enzyme. Because copper can't be absorbed normally, treatment uses injected copper plus liver extract and a celiac-type diet. In his words: "Menkes' Kinky Hair Syndrome is thought to be a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption. The affected infants exhibit retarded growth, defective keratin formation of the hair, loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (low thyroid function, anemia), degeneration and fractures of aortic elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of long bones, and a progressive mental deterioration. Mental deterioration results from brain tissue being totally devoid of the essential copper dependent enzyme cytochrome oxidase."
claims.verbatim:
Menkes’ Kinky Hair Syndrome is thought to be a sex-linked recessive genetic defect of copper absorption. The affected
infants exhibit retarded growth, defective keratin formation
of the hair, loss of hair pigment, low body temperature (low
thyroid function, anemia), degeneration and fractures of aortic
elastin (aneurysms), arthritis in the growth plates of long bones,
and a progressive mental deterioration. Mental deterioration
results from brain tissue being totally devoid of the essential
copper dependent enzyme cytochrome oxidase.

claims.claim_text: Some situations that raise blood copper. Serum and plasma copper roughly double (increase 100%) in pregnant women and in women taking oral contraceptives (the pill), and rise during acute infections, liver disease, and pellagra (the disease of niacin / vitamin-B3 deficiency). When copper accumulates in the cornea of the eye it forms visible Kayser-Fleischer rings — a classic sign of copper overload. In his words: "Serum and plasma copper increases 100% in pregnant women and women using oral contraceptives. Serum copper levels are also elevated during acute infections, liver disease, and pellagra (niacin deficiency). Accumulations of copper in the cornea form Kayser-Fleischer Rings."
claims.verbatim:
Serum and plasma copper increases 100% in pregnant
women and women using oral contraceptives. Serum copper
levels are also elevated during acute infections, liver disease,
and pellagra (niacin deficiency).

Accumulations of copper in the cornea form Kayser-Fleischer Rings.

claims.claim_text: Dysprosium is a rare earth element and, Wallach notes, the ninth most abundant of the rare earths. It was discovered in 1886 by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran while working with a sample of erbium oxide, and named from the Greek dysprositos — 'hard to get at.' It's a soft, shiny, silvery metal (soft enough to cut with a knife) that is fairly stable in air, and its magnetic alloys are used to help compact discs (CDs) work efficiently. In the body it accumulates in the bones. In his words: "Of the rare earths, dysprosium is a metal that ranks ninth in abundance. It was discovered in 1886 by the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran who was working with a sample of erbium oxide. It was named for the Greek word dysprositos, which translates to 'hard to get at.'"
claims.verbatim:
Of the rare earths, dysprosium is a metal that ranks
ninth in abundance. It was discovered in 1886 by the French
chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran who was working
with a sample of erbium oxide. It was named for the Greek
word dysprositos, which translates to “hard to get at.”

claims.claim_text: Erbium is a scarce rare earth metal, discovered in 1843 by the Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander; in its ores it occurs as an impurity among the other rare earths. Industrially, erbium is alloyed with metals like vanadium to improve their workability, and — its most memorable use — it is added to glass and enamel to tint them pink, the pink glass being used for sunglasses and costume jewelry. In the body it concentrates mainly in bone. In his words: "Erbium is employed in special alloys with metals such as vanadium to improve their workability characteristics. Erbium is frequently added to glass and enamel to tint them pink, this glass is commonly used for sunglasses and costume jewelry."
claims.verbatim:
Erbium is employed in special alloys with metals such
as vanadium to improve their workability characteristics.
Erbium is frequently added to glass and enamel to tint them
pink, this glass is commonly used for sunglasses and costume
jewelry.

claims.claim_text: Europium is a 'light' rare earth and one of the rarest of all the rare earth elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay, who named it for the continent of Europe. It is the softest of the rare earths and so reactive it ignites spontaneously in air above 150°C. It occurs in the ores monazite and bastnäsite — monazite (found in the river sands of India and Brazil and in Florida beach sand) carries all the rare earths plus thorium and calcium, and large bastnäsite deposits sit in Southern California. In his words: "Europium is one of the most-rare of the rare earth elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who named the new element for the continent of Europe."
claims.verbatim:
Europium is one of the most-rare of the rare earth
elements. It was isolated in 1901 by the French chemist
Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who named the new element for
the continent of Europe.

claims.claim_text: This is europium's headline claim, and it sits squarely in the book's anti-aging theme: Wallach says europium supplementation extended the life expectancy of laboratory species by 100% — doubling their lifespan beyond what was expected. That is one of the largest lifespan-extension figures in the book. He pairs it with a pointed nutritional observation: europium is more concentrated in the breast milk of women in third-world countries than in American women — his implication being that the modern American diet is the more depleted one. In his words: "Europium supplementation has extended the life expectancy of laboratory species over their expected lifespan by 100%. Europium is found in higher concentrations in breast milk from women in third world countries than in American women."
claims.verbatim:
Europium supplementation has extended the life
expectancy of laboratory species over their expected lifespan
by 100%. Europium is found in higher concentrations in breast
milk from women in third world countries than in American
women.

claims.claim_text: Fluorine is a halogen — the family Wallach calls the 'salt formers,' which also includes chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. These elements react by grabbing electrons from other atoms and readily combine with metals to make salts. Fluorine is the smallest, lightest and most reactive of the whole family — a pale-yellow gas whose molecules pair up into two atoms (diatomic), and so reactive it never occurs free in nature; it's found instead locked in minerals like fluorite (calcium fluoride, also called fluorspar). In his words: "Fluorine is a member of the halogen family or 'salt formers.' The other members are chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. All halogen atoms react chemically by accepting electrons from other atoms and easily combine with metals to form compounds known as salts. Fluorine is the smallest, lightest and most reactive member of the halogen family."
claims.verbatim:
Fluorine is a member of the halogen family or “salt
formers.” The other members are chlorine, bromine, iodine
and astatine. All halogen atoms react chemically by accepting
electrons from other atoms and easily combine with metals
to form compounds known as salts. Fluorine is the smallest,
lightest and most reactive member of the halogen family.

claims.claim_text: The element's discovery. The French chemist Henri Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure elemental form — the culmination of 75 years of effort by many chemists, with Moissan finally isolating it in 1886. The name comes from the Latin fluere, 'to flow.' In his words: "The French chemist Henri Moissan won the Nobel Prize in 1906 for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure elemental form. The name fluorine is derived from the Latin word fluere, which translates to 'to flow.'"
claims.verbatim:
The French chemist Henri Moissan won the Nobel
Prize in 1906 for being the first to produce fluorine in its pure
elemental form. The name fluorine is derived from the Latin
word fluere, which translates to “to flow.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach's stance on fluoride's essentiality. Before 1972 fluoride was only 'considered' essential in animals, based on its apparent benefit to tooth enamel in warding off cavities. Then in 1972, Schwarz proved that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for both animals and humans. (Note: despite this, fluoride is not carried in this system's operational list of Wallach/Youngevity supplement essentials — see the full fluoride stance for why the picture is two-sided.) In his words: "Prior to 1972, fluoride was considered essential in animals because of its apparent benefit for tooth enamel in warding off dental caries ('cavities'). In 1972, Schwarz proved that fluoride was in fact an essential mineral for animals and humans."

claims.claim_text: How fluoride protects teeth — the mechanism behind fluoride toothpaste. Tooth enamel is made of a hard mineral, hydroxyapatite. Acids that mouth bacteria produce from sugary food and drink slowly dissolve it, and that loss of enamel starts tooth decay ('caries'). The body constantly fights back by rebuilding enamel (remineralization). When sodium fluoride is present, the rebuilt enamel forms as fluorapatite — a version considerably more resistant to acid damage than natural enamel. That acid-resistance is exactly why manufacturers add sodium fluoride to toothpaste. In his words: "The resulting loss of the hydroxyapatite enamel promotes the initiation of tooth decay or 'caries.' One of the body's defenses against the breakdown of hydroxyapatite is to generate new enamel continuously (remineralization). In the presence of sodium fluoride, the remineralization process manufactures a form of enamel referred to as fluorapatite. Fluorapatite is considerably more resistant to damage from acid than the natural enamel."

The resulting loss of the hydroxyapatite enamel


promotes the initiation of tooth decay or “caries.” One of the
body’s defenses against the breakdown of hydroxyapatite is

In the presence of sodium fluoride, the remineralization

The skeleton of an adult man can hold up to 2.6 grams (2,600 mg) of fluoride in reserve, and the average American takes in about 4.4 mg per day from the combination of food, water, toothpaste and nutritional supplements. In his words: "The skeletal reserves of fluoride in an adult man can reach 2.6 gm (2,600 mg); the average daily intake by Americans is 4.4 mg from combined sources of food, water, toothpaste and nutritional supplements."

claims.claim_text: Fluoride's toxicity thresholds — the other side of the mineral. Wallach lays out where fluoride becomes harmful by concentration: dental fluorosis (mottled, discolored teeth) appears at fluoride concentrations of 2 to 7 ppm; osteosclerosis (an abnormal hardening/thickening of bone) at 8 to 20 ppm; and chronic whole-body (systemic) toxicity when daily fluoride intake stays above 20 to 80 ppm for several years. In his words: "Clinical toxicity is observed as dental fluorosis at fluoride concentrations of 2 to 7 ppm and osteosclerosis at 8 to 20 ppm. Chronic systemic toxicity appears when the daily fluoride intake levels are above 20 to 80 ppm over several years."

Clinical toxicity
is observed as dental fluorosis at fluoride concentrations of 2

above 20 to 80 ppm over several years.

claims.claim_text: The scale of U.S. water fluoridation and its trade-off. About 10,000 American towns and cities — serving 100 million people — add fluoride to municipal drinking water at 1 mg/L (one part per million), which has reportedly cut dental cavities by 60 to 70%. But in certain western U.S. states the natural fluoride runs high — 10 to 45 ppm — with the visible result of mottled (fluorosis-stained) teeth in children. In his words: "Approximately 10,000 American towns and cities serving a total of 100 million people have added fluoride to their municipal drinking water at the rate of 1 mg/L, which has reportedly reduced dental caries by 60 to 70%. In certain western states in the U.S., there is an excess of fluoride, reaching levels of 10 to 45 ppm with a resultant mottling of teeth in children."

claims.claim_text: The fluoride-cancer studies Wallach cites. Epidemiological work by Yiamouyiannis and Burk in 1977 led to full-scale U.S. congressional hearings over the charge that fluoridation of public water systems had caused 10,000 excess cancer deaths. The hearings ordered the U.S. National Toxicology Program to run animal studies focused on oral, liver and skeletal cancers. In 1990 those results showed, in rats, an increase in precancerous lesions of mucous-membrane cells; an increase in cancers of the oral mucous membranes (squamous cell carcinoma); a rare osteosarcoma (bone cancer) appearing at double the rate in males as in females; and increases in thyroid follicular-cell tumors and in liver cancer (hepatocholangiocarcinoma). In his words: "In 1990, the results of the fluoride study showed an increase in rat precancerous lesions in mucus membrane cells. There was an increase in cancers of the oral mucus membranes (squamous cell carcinoma). A rare form of osteosarcoma appeared at double the rate in males as females, and there was an increase in thyroid follicular cell tumors and liver cancer (hepatocholangiocarcinoma)."

In 1990, the results of the fluoride study showed an

There was an increase in cancers of the oral mucus membranes

appeared at double the rate in males as females, and there was
an increase in thyroid follicular cell tumors and liver cancer
(hepatocholangiocarcinoma).

claims.claim_text: Wallach's full stance on fluoride — why it sounds both essential and dangerous, made clear. WHAT IT IS: fluoride is the most reactive halogen and, per a 1972 study by Schwarz, a nutritionally essential trace mineral for animals and humans. ITS REAL BENEFIT: fluoride hardens tooth enamel — teeth rebuild it as acid-resistant fluorapatite, which fights the cavities caused by sugar-fed mouth bacteria; that is why it's in toothpaste, and water fluoridation (~1 mg/L) has reportedly cut cavities 60–70%. ITS REAL HARMS: fluoride is also toxic above trace levels — dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) at 2–7 ppm, osteosclerosis (abnormal bone hardening) at 8–20 ppm, and chronic systemic toxicity above 20–80 ppm/day over years — and Wallach cites studies (Yiamouyiannis & Burk 1977; the U.S. National Toxicology Program's 1990 rat study) tying fluoridation to excess cancer deaths and to oral, bone (osteosarcoma), thyroid and liver tumors. HOW IT'S BOTH — the reconciliation: the dose makes the poison. Fluoride is essential only in tiny amounts (the whole adult skeleton holds ~2.6 g; average intake ~4.4 mg/day), while the harms appear at higher, sustained exposure — so 'essential in trace' and 'toxic in excess' are the same mineral at different doses, not a contradiction. ON WATER FLUORIDATION: Wallach calls it 'still highly controversial' and presents both sides — the cavity benefit versus the fluorosis, bone and cancer concerns, even noting that studies disagree on whether fluoridated water reduces or increases bone fractures. In this passage he lays out the debate and flags the toxicity/cancer evidence rather than issuing a flat yes-or-no verdict on whether you should drink it. In his words: "The universal fluoridation of drinking water is still highly controversial. Some studies show that fluoridated water helps reduce fractures from osteoporosis, while other studies showed an increase in hip fractures."

The universal fluoridation of drinking water is still

water helps reduce fractures from osteoporosis, while other
studies showed an increase in hip fractures.

claims.claim_text: How abundant iron is, and its place in human history. Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and the second most abundant metal (after aluminum); its content is responsible for most soil color, and the planet's molten core is thought to be magnetized iron. Learning to smelt iron from its red-brown ores (mainly hematite and magnetite) was a milestone that opened the Iron Age (~1100 B.C.), giving humanity tools and weapons harder than those of the earlier Bronze Age; today iron makes up about 90% of all metal extracted from ore. In his words: "Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the earth's crust and is second only to aluminum as the most abundant metal. The 'core' or interior of the earth is theorized to be made up of magnetized, molten iron."

Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the earth’s
crust and is second only to aluminum as the most abundant
metal. The “core” or interior of the earth is theorized to be
made up of magnetized, molten iron.

claims.claim_text: Why iron is essential — it is what lets your blood carry oxygen. Iron is an essential nutrient for all land animals. Each hemoglobin molecule (the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells) is built around four iron atoms; oxygen chemically bonds to those iron atoms in the tiny blood vessels of the lungs (capillaries) and is then carried through the circulation to cells throughout the body. Iron was first recognized as an essential animal nutrient by Boussingault in the 1860s. In his words: "Iron is an essential nutrient for all terrestrial species of animals. It is the four iron atoms in each hemoglobin molecule that are central to its structure and physiological function. Oxygen actually bonds to the iron atoms in the lung capillaries, and then are transported via the circulation to distant cells."

Iron is an essential nutrient for all terrestrial species
of animals. It is the four iron atoms in each hemoglobin
molecule that are central to its structure and physiological
function. Oxygen actually bonds to the iron atoms in the lung
capillaries, and then are transported via the circulation to
distant cells.

claims.claim_text: Why carbon monoxide is so deadly — it hijacks iron's oxygen seat. Carbon monoxide, a gas produced by incomplete burning of fuel, binds to the iron in hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than oxygen does. Because it clings so hard, it crowds oxygen out of the blood — which is what makes carbon monoxide poisoning dangerous. In his words: "Carbon monoxide, a byproduct of imperfect combustion, is bound to the hemoglobin iron 200 times more tightly than oxygen - this phenomenon can lead to 'carbon monoxide poisoning!'"

tightly than oxygen - this phenomenon can lead to “carbon
monoxide poisoning!”

claims.claim_text: How much iron your body holds, and where it sits. A healthy adult carries about 3 to 5 grams of iron, and a newborn has nearly twice as much per kilogram of body weight as an adult. Roughly 60 to 70% is 'functional' iron doing active work — in hemoglobin, in muscle's oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin, and in the cell's respiratory enzymes — while 30 to 40% is held in reserve as storage iron (as ferritin and hemosiderin in the bone marrow and liver). In his words: "In a healthy adult human there is three to five grams of iron, the newborn infant has nearly double the amount of iron per kg than adults. Sixty to 70% of tissue iron is used as essential or functional iron, and 30 to 40% as storage iron."

In a healthy adult human there is three to five grams
of iron, the newborn infant has nearly double the amount of
iron per kg than adults. Sixty to 70% of tissue iron is used as
essential or functional iron, and 30 to 40% as storage iron.

claims.claim_text: Pica — cravings to eat non-foods — is a specific sign of iron deficiency. Wallach says the experimental evidence shows clearly that 'pica' points specifically to a lack of iron. The pica drive can push children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead paint, excess food ('the munchies,' leading to obesity), alcohol (alcoholism), and sugar (a 'sweet tooth'). In his words: "Experimental evidence shows very clearly that 'pica' is a specific sign of iron deficiency. The pica behavior can drive children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia), dirt (geophagia), lead paint, excess food ('munchies,' obesity), alcohol (alcoholism) and sugar (sweet tooth)."
